records.title: Effects of muscle strength training combined with aerobic training versus aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.

content.title: Effects of muscle strength training combined with aerobic training versus aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To compare the effects of aerobic training combined with muscle strength training (hereafter referred to as combined training) to aerobic training alone on cardiovascular disease risk indicators in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD).

Design

Systematic review with meta-analysis.

Data sources

MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, trial registries and grey literature sources were searched in February 2024.

Eligibility criteria

Randomised clinical trials comparing the effects of ≥4 weeks of combined training and aerobic training alone on at least one of the following outcomes: cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), anthropometric and haemodynamic measures and cardiometabolic blood biomarkers in patients with CAD.

Results

Of 13 246 studies screened, 23 were included (N=916). Combined training was more effective in increasing CRF (standard mean difference (SMD) 0.26, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.49, p=0.03) and lean body mass (mean difference (MD) 0.78 kg, 95% CI 0.39 kg to 1.17 kg, p<0.001), and reducing per cent body fat (MD -2.2%, 95% CI -3.5% to -0.9%, p=0.001) compared with aerobic training alone. There were no differences in the cardiometabolic biomarkers between the groups. Our subgroup analyses showed that combined training increases CRF more than aerobic training alone when muscle strength training was added to aerobic training without compromising aerobic training volume (SMD 0.36, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.68, p=0.02).

Conclusion

Combined training had greater effects on CRF and body composition than aerobic training alone in patients with CAD. To promote an increase in CRF in patients with CAD, muscle strength training should be added to aerobic training without reducing aerobic exercise volume.

records.title: Impact of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related indices in patients with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

content.title: Impact of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related indices in patients with type 2 diabetes and overweight/obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objective

To evaluate the effects of resistance training on cardiometabolic health-related outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and overweight/obesity.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs).

Data sources

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Science Direct, Cochrane Library and Google Scholar databases were searched from inception up to May 2024. The search strategy included the following keywords: diabetes, resistance exercise and strength training.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

RCTs published in English comparing resistance training alone with non-exercising standard treatment. Participants were adults diagnosed with T2DM and concurrent overweight/obesity (body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m2).

Results

A total of 18 RCTs qualified involving 1180 patients (48.6/51.4 female/male ratio; 63.3±7.0 years; 29.3±4.3 kg/m2). Waist circumference (standardised mean differences (SMD) -0.85 cm, 95% CI -1.66 to -0.04), waist-to-hip ratio (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.30 to -0.15), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (SMD +0.40 mg/dL, 95% CI 0.07 to -0.72), triglycerides (SMD -0.54 mg/dL, 95% CI -1.06 to -0.02), fasting blood glucose (SMD -0.65 mmol/L, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.12), fasting insulin (SMD -0.74 uIU/mL, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.36) and glycated haemoglobin (SMD -0.32%, 95% CI -0.63 to -0.01) improved compared with standard treatment. The risk of bias was low to unclear, and the quality of evidence was very low to moderate.

Conclusions

Resistance training as a standalone exercise intervention in the management and treatment of T2DM with concurrent overweight/obesity is associated with many cardiometabolic benefits when compared with standard treatment without exercise.

Prospero registration number

CRD42022355612.

records.title: Grading the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.

content.title: Grading the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.
content.abstract:
Objective

To synthesise the evidence on the effects of exercise interventions in children and adolescents during and beyond cancer treatment, and to evaluate the methodological quality and certainty of this evidence.

Design

Umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.

Data source

PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and CINAHL were searched from inception to January 2026.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Systematic reviews with meta-analysis of controlled trials (randomised or non-randomised) evaluating exercise interventions in children and adolescents (≤19 years) during and beyond cancer treatment. Reviews without quantitative synthesis, those including only observational studies, or interventions where the isolated effect of exercise could not be determined were excluded.

Results

19 systematic reviews with meta-analyses, including 53 primary studies (n=2361 participants), were identified, yielding 80 effect estimates. Attending to the most comprehensive meta-analyses, exercise induced significant benefits on cardiorespiratory fitness (mean difference (MD) 6.92% (95% CI 1.01% to 12.82%)), cognitive function (standardised mean difference (SMD) 0.26 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.44)) and cognitive performance (SMD 0.41 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.65)), with moderate certainty of evidence. Exercise also induced significant benefits on muscle strength (SMD 0.81 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.57)), functional mobility (MD -1.17 s (95% CI -1.86 to -0.49)) and cancer-related fatigue (SMD -0.62 (95% CI -1.21 to -0.03)), although the certainty was low or very low. These effects were observed across meta-analyses focused exclusively on studies conducted during treatment (n=26), after treatment (n=3) or both (n=51). In contrast, no significant effects of exercise were observed for depression, bone mineral density, health-related quality of life, anthropometry or other clinical outcomes (such as mortality, relapse risk and withdrawal rates).

Conclusion

Exercise appears to be a beneficial intervention in childhood cancer for improving some physical, cognitive and psychosocial outcomes. However, more high-quality research is warranted to strengthen clinical recommendations and inform personalised exercise prescriptions, given that the certainty of evidence remains variable and overall low across outcomes.

Prospero registration number

CRD420251031412.

records.title: Clinical importance of simple muscular fitness tests to predict long-term health conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 94 cohort studies.

content.title: Clinical importance of simple muscular fitness tests to predict long-term health conditions: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 94 cohort studies.
content.abstract:
Objective

To examine the predictive validity of field-based muscular strength tests in relation to incident long-term health conditions among adults.

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis.

Data sources

PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Scopus, CINAHL, Epistemonikos and Google Scholar.

Eligibility criteria

Cohort studies examining the predictive value of validated and/or reliable field-based muscular strength tests in relation to long-term health conditions in adults aged ≥18 years.

Results

A total of 155 studies were included with 94 included in the meta-analysis. Adults with the highest (vs lowest) handgrip strength levels had a lower risk of multiple long-term health conditions (all p<0.05), including cardiovascular diseases (OR=0.73; 95% CI 0.67 to 0.80), type 2 diabetes mellitus (OR=0.79; 95% CI 0.68 to 0.91), musculoskeletal impairment (OR=0.65; 95% CI 0.56 to 0.76), disability (OR=0.57; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.70), anxiety (OR=0.79; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.99), depression (OR=0.70; 95% CI 0.63 to 0.78), cognitive decline (OR=0.57; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.75), dementia (OR=0.62; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.73) and Parkinson's disease (OR=0.53; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.91). A 5 kg increase in handgrip strength was associated with a lower risk of developing most of these long-term health conditions. In turn, adults with the best (vs worst) performance on the 5-repetition chair-stand test had a lower risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus (OR=0.80; 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88), musculoskeletal impairment (OR=0.52; 95% CI 0.37 to 0.74), disability (OR=0.58; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.82), depression (OR=0.63; 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95), and dementia (OR=0.68; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85). Every 1 s decrease was associated with 0.94 lower odds of musculoskeletal impairment. The overall quality of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, indicating limited to moderate confidence in the results.

Conclusions

Our findings suggest increased handgrip strength and chair-stand test performance are associated with a lower risk of multiple long-term health conditions among adults. This research underscores the predictive value of simple field-based muscular strength tests which appear to be clinically useful for adults across different age groups and demographic profiles.

records.title: Efficacy of exercise interventions on prevention of sport-related concussion and related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy of exercise interventions on prevention of sport-related concussion and related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

To review the efficacy of exercise interventions on sport-related concussion (SRC) incidence, as well as on linear and rotational head accelerations, and isometric neck strength and to assess reporting completeness of exercise interventions using the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template (CERT).

Design

Systematic review and meta-analysis, according to the Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science guidelines.

Data sources

Six databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science CC and SPORTDiscus) were searched up to 26 June 2023.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs or quasi-experimental studies, evaluating exercise interventions on SRC incidence, linear and rotational head accelerations, and/or isometric neck strength in male and/or female athletes of any age, and/or in a healthy general population.

Results

A total of 26 articles were included. A large effect size was observed for resistance training (RT) on isometric neck strength (standardised mean difference (SMD) 0.85; 95% CI 0.57 to 1.13; high-quality evidence). Non-significant effect sizes were observed for neuromuscular warm-up programmes on SRC incidence (risk ratio 0.69; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.23; low-quality evidence), or for RT on linear head acceleration (SMD -0.43; 95% CI -1.26 to 0.40; very low-quality evidence) or rotational head acceleration (SMD 0.08; 95% CI -0.61 to 0.77; low-quality evidence). No studies assessed the impact of RT on SRC incidence. CERT scores ranged from 4 to 16 (out of 19) with median score of 11.5 (IQR 9-13).

Conclusion

RT increases isometric neck strength, but the effect on SRC incidence is unknown. More adequately powered and rigorous trials are needed to evaluate the effect of exercise interventions on SRC incidence, and on linear and rotational head accelerations. Future studies should follow CERT guidelines, as the included interventions were generally not reported in sufficient detail for accurate replication.

records.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Human Multi-Omics Meta-Analysis Identifies Molecular Layer-Specific Responses to Resistance and Endurance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Resistance and endurance exercise produce distinct adaptations, but molecular responses that distinguish these exercise modalities across studies and molecular layers remain incompletely defined. We sought to identify reproducible resistance- and endurance-associated molecular responses across human skeletal muscle and plasma omics datasets.

Methods

We integrated publicly available human exercise omics datasets. Random-effects meta-analyses included 15,312 genes from three skeletal muscle RNA-seq datasets and 4,641 proteins from two skeletal muscle proteomic datasets. Early skeletal muscle phosphoproteomic responses were compared across two independent studies using 2,430 matched phosphosites. At 24 hours, skeletal muscle phosphoproteomics and targeted and untargeted metabolomics in skeletal muscle and plasma were analyzed separately; plasma proteomics was not analyzed. Effects were standardized as resistance exercise minus endurance exercise, with significance defined within each molecular layer at FDR<0.05.

Results

RNA-seq identified 269 genes, including 71 resistance-associated and 198 endurance-associated genes. Global proteomics identified 10 proteins (nine resistance-associated; one endurance-associated). Early phosphoproteomic effects correlated across studies (r=0.589, P=4.1x10-227); 210 of 238 significant phosphosites were directionally concordant, and 51 met replication criteria. At 24 hours, targeted plasma metabolomics identified 14 endurance-associated features, while untargeted plasma metabolomics identified 18 features, including nine resistance-associated and nine endurance-associated features. Resistance-associated responses involved contractile, myofibrillar, cytoskeletal, extracellular matrix, protein quality-control, stress-response, and phosphorylation-related processes. Endurance-associated responses involved mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, respiratory-chain biology, fatty acid oxidation, substrate utilization, amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial proteostasis.

Conclusions

Human molecular responses to resistance and endurance exercise are molecular-layer specific. Endurance-associated responses were more consistently represented in transcriptomic and metabolic layers, whereas resistance-associated responses were more prominent in protein abundance and phosphorylation. These findings provide a quantitative basis for selecting molecular measurements and sampling strategies in future human resistance and endurance exercise studies.

records.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

records.title: Acute caffeine and carbohydrate strategies for fatigue-related sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes: a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Acute caffeine and carbohydrate strategies for fatigue-related sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes: a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Although caffeine and carbohydrate are established ergogenic strategies for physical performance, it remains unclear whether these benefits translate to the decision-making and sport-specific skills that determine team-sport performance under fatigue.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and SPORTDiscus were searched on 28 July 2026. Thirty-one reports were retained; their reported analyzed sample sizes summed to 441 athletes. Twenty-three independent quantitative study clusters, with reported analyzed sample sizes summing to 341 athletes, contributed 67 effects. Multilevel random-effects models nested effect sizes within studies; primary assumptions were r = 0.5 and rho = 0.80. Inference used CR2 robust standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

Results

Soccer supplied 11 of the 23 quantitative clusters; every other sport category supplied four or fewer. Broad caffeine was centered near zero (Hedges' g = 0.040, 95% CI -0.211 to 0.291; p = 0.691; df = 4.41). Tier 1a perceptual-motor and Tier 1b technical/tactical estimates were imprecise. Broad carbohydrate was positive but uncertain (g = 0.256, 95% CI -0.094 to 0.605; p = 0.118; df = 4.96), and one study cluster materially influenced this estimate. All six GRADE comparisons were rated very low certainty. The two-study mental-fatigue calculation was too fragile for conventional inference.

Conclusions

Current evidence does not support assuming that the established physical ergogenic effects of caffeine translate to fatigue-related decision-making or sport-specific skill. Carbohydrate may provide a small benefit, but the evidence remains sparse and highly uncertain. Sensitivity to study composition was driven primarily by one influential cluster, whose omission increased the pooled estimate. The carbohydrate estimates apply only to heterogeneous ingested-beverage protocols and should not be extrapolated to mouth-rinse or gel strategies. Parallel syntheses do not establish intervention superiority or combined-strategy synergy.

records.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
content.abstract:
Abstract

So, YLI, Faricier, R, Guluzade, NA, Belfry, GR, Murias, JM, and Keir, DA. The respiratory compensation point predicts 19.2-km cycling performance in trained male cyclists. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study tested the hypothesis that the step-ramp-step (SRS)-corrected cycling power output (PO) at the respiratory compensation point (RCP) predicts cycling time-trial performance and explored the independent and collective contributions to trial time of 4 physiological variables derived from single or repeated SRS protocols: peak oxygen uptake (V̇o2peak), cycling economy, RCP, and fatigue resistance. Twenty-eight trained male cyclists completed an SRS protocol before and after a 19.2-km virtual time trial (∼30 minutes) on their personal road bikes using a smart trainer. V̇o2peak, cycling economy, and SRS-corrected PO at RCP were derived from the pre-time-trial SRS protocol. Fatigue resistance was quantified as the change in peak ramp PO from pre- to post-time trial. Independent and multilinear regression evaluated the predictive strength of each variable. Relative SRS-corrected RCP (W·kg-1) showed the strongest independent correlation with time-trial completion time (r = -0.61, p < 0.001). Relative V̇o2peak (mL·kg-1·min-1) and cycling economy (%) were also moderately associated with time-trial performance (r = -0.42, p = 0.03; and r = -0.55, p < 0.001, respectively), whereas fatigue resistance was not significantly correlated. In the multilinear regression analysis, SRS-corrected RCP uniquely explained 30.9% of the model's total predictive variance (r = 0.68, p < 0.01) followed by cycling economy (21.3%), ΔPOpeak (2.1%), and absolute V̇o2peak (3.3%). Among trained male cyclists, relative PO at SRS-corrected RCP is a strong and independent predictor of ∼30-minute time-trial performance. The SRS protocol provides a practical, single-session method to assess key physiological determinants of endurance performance, with valuable applications for training prescription and athlete monitoring.

records.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Background

Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.

Methods

Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.

Results

CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.

Conclusions

Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

records.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Moderate-Intensity Interval Training Is Sufficient to Increase Muscle Mitochondrial Respiratory Capacity and Exercise Tolerance in Young Untrained Men.
content.abstract:
Introduction

There is considerable evidence that physical activity can stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in muscles, enhance maximal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate, improve physical fitness, and help maintain overall health in humans. On the other hand, there is growing evidence that excessive training load may have a detrimental effect on mitochondria and glucose homeostasis.

Hypothesis

We hypothesized that moderate-intensity interval training (MIIT) would be sufficient to increase muscle mitochondrial oxidative capacity and exercise tolerance in untrained healthy people.

Methods

Eleven young, healthy, untrained males took part in this study. They performed a 7-week endurance training program (MIIT) on a cycle ergometer, composed of 4 sessions per week, each lasting 40 min. Before and after the MIIT training program, a pulmonary maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) as well as lactate threshold (LT) were determined and a muscle biopsy from the m. vastus lateralis was taken to evaluate the level of muscle proteins related to energy metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis, and to measure the muscle's maximal mitochondrial respiration rate.

Results

The training resulted in an increase of skeletal muscle homogenate V̇O2max (by ~50%, P=0.001), due to increased mitochondrial mass and the enrichment of mitochondria with the individual respiratory chain complexes. The MIIT increased the power output at the lactate threshold (PO at LT) by ~43 W (P=0.001) and the pulmonary V̇O2max by 7% (P=0.01) and had no adverse effect on blood glucose homeostasis.

Conclusions

MIIT, which is a less intense form of training than the commonly used types of interval training, effectively induces a range of beneficial muscular and systemic adaptations that contribute to improvement of physical fitness and maintenances good health in humans.

records.title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

records.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Sex-specific Lower Limb Strength, Flexibility, and Running Biomechanics in Adolescents With and Without Osgood-Schlatter Disease.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To examine sex-specific lower limb strength, flexibility, and running biomechanics in adolescents with and without OSD.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective chart review of 100 adolescents (n=25 each group): females with OSD (age=14.6 ± 1.9 y; body mass index [BMI]=21.3 ± 2.1 kg/m2); males with OSD (age=14.4 ± 1.6 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2); females without OSD (age=14.8 ± 2.2 y; BMI=21.7 ± 3.0 kg/m2); and males without OSD (age=14.4 ± 2.2 y; BMI=22.0 ± 4.6 kg/m2). We assessed mass-normalized sagittal and frontal hip strength and sagittal knee strength via hand-held dynamometry, and quadriceps femoris (prone knee flexion) and hip flexor (Thomas test) flexibility. Limb crossover, contralateral pelvic drop [CPD], medial knee displacement, and tibial dominant stride were assessed during treadmill running. Group differences were analyzed using a two-way multivariate analysis of variance (continuous outcomes) and logistic regression (categorical outcomes), covarying for age and BMI. Analyses were performed using SPSS (alpha set at p<0.05).

Results

Compared with sex-matched healthy peers, females with OSD had impaired hip abduction strength and a greater propensity for CPD and medial knee displacement, though greater hip flexion strength (p≤0.03; Table). Males with OSD had greater hip and knee sagittal plane strength yet impaired flexibility (p≤0.02; Table). Compared with males with OSD, females with OSD had lower hip and knee strength, greater quadriceps femoris flexibility, and higher odds of frontal plane biomechanical deficits (p≤0.02; Table).

Conclusion

We observed sex-specific differences in lower limb muscular and biomechanical features in adolescents with OSD, suggesting that clinicians should consider sex-specific rehabilitation strategies for adolescents with OSD.

records.title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
content.abstract:
Introduction

Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations.

Purpose

To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint.

Methods

55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed.

Results

At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric).

Conclusions

Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

records.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Should They Start or Not? A Comparative Analysis of Starter and Nonstarter Preseason Fitness Characteristics in NCAA Division III Baseball.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Schilling, DT, Abraham, TR, and Elazzazi, A. Should they start or not? A comparative analysis of starter and nonstarter preseason fitness characteristics in NCAA Division III baseball. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Preseason fitness testing in baseball is a widely adopted practice to assess the physical preparedness of players. However, the relationship between these preseason fitness assessments, their ability to differentiate starters from nonstarters in the subsequent season, and their relationship to preseason coaching evaluations is not well-established. This exploratory study aimed to provide a preseason profile of men's NCAA Division III baseball players, compare the differences between starting and nonstarting players, and explore the relationship of these preseason measures to the offensive performance of the starting players at the completion of the season. Starters were considered any hitter who averaged at least 2 plate appearances per team game played or participated in at least 75% of the team's games. Twenty-six players performed 8 preseason fitness tests; and the head coach, blinded to all preseason fitness testing results, subjectively rated the players' batting (power, ball contact, and form) and running performance (speed, agility, and form), resulting in a total offensive performance score (TOPS). In-season offensive performance was measured by each player's on-base plus slugging percentage (OPS). Starters demonstrated significantly greater batted ball velocity, countermovement vertical jump height, unilateral lateral to medial jump distance, medicine ball throw velocity, and faster 60-yard dash and agility T-test times relative to nonstarters. Notably, no significant correlations were observed between any physical performance variable and OPS or TOPS, suggesting that preseason fitness testing may reflect athletic readiness but does not directly relate to offensive performance or coaching evaluation outcomes in this sample.

records.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
content.abstract:
Background

This study investigated the effects of three doses of caffeine (CAF) on hematological and biochemical responses during the CrossFit® workout, a protocol known to induce significant physiological fluctuations.

Methods

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled crossover trial, 26 moderately trained CrossFit® athletes received acute doses of 3, 6, or 9 mgCAF/kgbody mass (BM), or a PLA, 70 min before a 17-min CrossFit® workout.

Results

While exercise was the predominant driver of hematological changes, with no CAF-specific modulation of blood cell indices, significant treatment × time point interactions were observed solely for glucose concentration. Specifically, MEDIUM (6 mgCAF/kgBM) and HIGH (9 mgCAF/kgBM) CAF doses produced significantly greater post-exercise glucose elevations compared to baseline and PLA visits. Phosphates concentrations increased over time, particularly post-exercise, with no treatment effect retained after excluding baseline visit in the sensitivity analysis. Calcium level dynamics were influenced by temporal factors rather than CAF, and magnesium concentration remained stable.

Conclusions

These findings suggest that acute CAF ingestion selectively influences post-exercise glucose responses during the CrossFit® workout, whereas hematological variables and most biochemical markers remain unaffected. Significant post-exercise glucose elevations were observed following the 6 and 9 mgCAF/kgBM conditions compared with baseline and PLA visits, while serum mineral concentrations remained largely stable across treatments.

Clinical trials registration

NCT03822663.

records.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults.

Methods

Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires.

Results

There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments.

Conclusions

A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

records.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
content.abstract:
Purpose

To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.

Methods

Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.

Results

Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.

Conclusions

The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

records.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of milk fat globule membrane supplementation on physical function and body composition in older adults: a narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Healthy aging is a priority for many individuals; however, a decline in physical function and poor body composition are common age-related changes that can cause the added years from rising life expectancy to be spent in poor health. Consequently, understanding the mechanisms involved in aging has become increasingly important, including the role of phospholipids (PLs) and how age-related changes in PL content may interfere with lipid metabolism and normal functioning of the musculoskeletal system. Milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) is a bovine milk fraction rich in PLs that may have the potential to support good physical health, so that quality of life can rise alongside life expectancy.

Methods

This narrative review was based on a literature search conducted on Google Scholar, PubMed, and Scopus in May 2026 using the following keywords and Boolean operators: milk fat globule membrane OR MFGM AND physical function OR body composition OR older adults. Studies were included if they were randomized clinical trials (RCTs) investigating MFGM's effects on physical function and/or body composition in older adults.

Results

Findings suggest that MFGM supplementation, when consumed in conjunction with exercise, is an effective way to improve physical function in older adults, particularly among Japanese cohorts; however, changes in habitual diet in response to exercise, variable PL concentrations, and other added ingredients used in interventions may have influenced these results. In contrast, its effects on body composition appear more modest, with some studies reporting no benefits, especially when exercise was not part of the study design, or when compliance may have been a factor.

Conclusions

Beyond the combined use of supplementation and exercise, future RCTs should consistently report participant compliance and, where possible, examine MFGM as a standalone intervention to distinguish its effects from other bioactive ingredients. Greater standardization is also needed, particularly regarding PL dose. Studies should also aim to include participants from more diverse ethnic backgrounds to capture a wider range of physiological responses and improve generalizability of the findings.

records.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
content.abstract:
Background

Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed.

Results

SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605).

Conclusions

Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

records.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Hammond, KG, Bair, AC, Strang, AJ, Young, JC, Kruskall, LJ, Dunnick, DD, and Schilling, BK. Feasibility of heart rate-based total daily energy expenditure estimation of pararescuemen in garrison. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Pararescuemen are a group of Air Force Special Operations Forces who engage in vigorous daily training to prepare for deployment operations. This training can elicit high-energy expenditure, yet few studies have measured the energy expenditure of these airmen while at their home station (in garrison). Twelve operational pararescuemen (age: 27 ± 3 years; years of service: 5 ± 3 years) were assessed for resting energy expenditure, heart rate (HR) at rest and during initial exercise, and the HR-oxygen consumption (V̇o2) linear equation. Subjects' HR was recorded over 2 normal training days and used to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Subjects reported an average 9 ± 2 hours of sleep per night of analysis and had an average basal metabolic rate = 82 ± 4 kcal·h-1. Average TDEE was 4,021 ± 890 kcals. Pararescuemen expend high levels of energy during routine training at their home station, similar to those of other elite military groups. Observed and reported high-energy expenditures in pararescuemen suggest further investigation into energy intake in this population to optimize performance.

records.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Payne, LKD, Varley, MC, Carey, DL, Driller, MW, and James, LP. Dimensionality reduction of full-body strength-power metrics to identify distinct strength domains in elite rugby union athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to determine the extent of shared and unique information among strength tests and to evaluate whether factors identified through exploratory factor analysis reflect distinct strength domains in professional rugby union players. Twenty professional male rugby union athletes (age 24.4 ± 3.8 years; height 186.3 ± 5.2 cm; body mass 107.6 ± 10.9 kg) completed a battery of 4 upper-body and 5 lower-body isometric, dynamic, and reactive strength tests. A total of 18 metrics were entered into exploratory factor analysis to identify distinct strength domains. Exploratory factor analysis reduced the data set into 2 upper-body domains (pressing and pulling) and 4 lower-body domains (isometric, dynamic, reactive, and relative). These domains together explained 73% of the variance in the upper-body data and 79% of the variance in the lower-body data. The isometric domain was driven by early-phase force at 100 and 200 ms, while peak force contributed less strongly. The dynamic domain was defined by heavy squat velocity, which diverged inversely from countermovement jump height, reflecting load-velocity differences. The reactive domain was shaped by contact time and countermovement depth, highlighting the role of temporal mechanics. The relative domain was defined by drop jump height and countermovement jump momentum, emphasizing the influence of body mass on ballistic force expression. Eighteen test metrics were successfully reduced to 6 distinct domains of strength in professional rugby union athletes. This framework provides a concise basis for profiling upper-body and lower-body strength to reduce redundancy and retain key information needed for training and monitoring rugby athletes.

records.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

records.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness as Mediator in the Association Between Physical Activity and Health-Related Quality of Life in Patients with CMD or OA.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Diseases like cardiovascular metabolic disease (CMD) and osteoarthritis (OA) impact health-related quality of life (hr-QoL). In the general population, hr-QoL is associated with physical activity (PA), sedentary time (ST) and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). This study aims to examine 1) associations between device-based and self-reported PA and ST, and hr-QoL, and 2) the influence of self-reported CRF in these associations in people with (or at risk for) CMD and/or OA.

Methods

Data from the Lifestyle front Office For Integrating lifestyle medicine in the Treatment of patients (LOFIT) study was used. Participants included patients with (or at risk for) CMD and/or OA (n=273) within the Netherlands. PA and ST were measured using device-based (activPAL™) and self-reported methods (International Physical Activity Questionnaire - Short Form and Marshall Sitting Questionnaire). CRF was assessed by estimating peak oxygen uptake per kilogram bodyweight (VO2peak mL·kg -1·min -1) using the FitMáx questionnaire. Hr-QoL was assessed using EQ-5D-5L. The associations were examined using linear regression and cross-sectional mediation models.

Results

Higher levels of device-based, and self-reported PA were associated with higher hr-QoL (b=0.007, 95% CI=0.000, 0.013 per 1000 steps, b=0.001 95% CI= 0.000, 0.002 per 30 minutes). Higher levels of device-based and self-reported ST were associated with lower hr-QoL (b=-0.006, 95% CI=-0.012, -0.000 per 30 minutes, b=-0.004, 95% CI=-0.007, -0.001 per 30 minutes). A cross-sectional indirect association via CRF was observed in the association between PA and hr-QoL.

Conclusions

Higher PA and lower ST are associated with enhanced hr-QoL, where CRF influences the relationship between PA and hr-QoL in this patient population. Reducing ST could be a more feasible first step, if increasing PA is challenging. Moreover, the influence of CRF emphasizes the need for interventions focusing on improving fitness levels.

records.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Ergocycling-Based Repeated-Sprint Training in Hypoxia Performed at Either 3,000 m or 2,000 m Similarly Impacts Overground Performance in Under-18 Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Le Moan, D, Slawinski, J, Lecru, L, Braize, E, Brocherie, F, and Bouten, J. Ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia performed at either 3,000 m or 2,000 m similarly impacts overground performance in under-18 field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to compare the effects of 2 levels of hypoxic stress during ergocycling-based repeated-sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) on overground repeated-sprint ability (RSA). Fifteen highly trained under-18 male field hockey players performed a 3-week training program with 6 ergocycling-based RSH sessions (3 × 6 10-s "all-out" sprints with 20-second intraset passive recovery and 5-minute interset rest; 2 sessions per week) under moderate (MH, FiO2 14.5%, simulated altitude of 3,000 m, n = 8) or low normobaric hypoxia (LH, FiO2 16.3%, 2,000 m, n = 7). Peak (PPO) and mean power output (MPO) were recorded during each RSH session. At Pre- and Postintervention, overground sprinting horizontal force-velocity profiles and RSA test (6 × 20-m "all-out" sprints interspersed by 20 seconds) were performed. Ergocycling-based PPO (p < 0.001) and MPO (p = 0.015) improved significantly for both groups from training 1 to 6. However, overground theoretical maximal force and theoretical maximal power remained unchanged (both p > 0.377), and theoretical maximal velocity (p = 0.026) was significantly decreased for both groups. Although no significant effect (time, group, interaction) was observed for overground RSA best time and sprint decrement (all p > 0.139), RSA total time decreased (p = 0.048) in both MH and LH (-1.1 ± 2.9% and -0.9 ± 1.0%), indicating performance enhancement, irrespective of the hypoxic stress. Using moderate or low normobaric hypoxic stress during a 3-week ergocycling-based RSH intervention resulted in similar improvement during training, albeit with limited, but not negligible, transferability effect in overground performance.

records.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Villaseca-Vicuña, R, Freitas, TT, Spyrou, K, Marín-Cascales, E, Comyns, T, Loturco, I, and Zabaloy, S. Countermovement jump performance across 10 competitive microcycles in under-18 soccer players: An analysis of delayed and long-term responses to training and official competition. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aims of this study were to (a) determine within-microcycle changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) measures (i.e., jump height, reactive strength index modified [RSImod], and eccentric peak velocity [EPV]) collected 2 days after (MD+2) and 1 day before (MD-1) the match-day across 10 weeks during the competitive period in under-18 soccer players and (b) analyze week-to-week variations in the selected CMJ-metrics collected on MD+2 across the entire mesocycle. Twelve (n = 12) under-18 academy soccer players (age: 17.5 ± 0.5 years; body mass: 71.9 ± 7.7 kg) volunteered to participate in this study. Over 10 competitive weeks, CMJ assessments were recorded on force plates at 2 key microcycle time points: MD+2 (active recovery phase at the start of the microcycle) and MD-1 (end of the microcycle). Results showed significant within-week changes in CMJ height and EPV in most of the training microcycles (p: <0.001 to 0.049) while RSImod showed significant changes in only 4 of the 10 microcycles (p: 0.001 to 0.049). Similarly, the between-week comparisons showed significant variations only in EPV and RSI (p: 0.005 to 0.049). These findings suggest that jump height might be better suited to assess within-week changes, while RSImod appears to hold greater discriminative value for detecting between-week fluctuations. Eccentric peak velocity, in turn, may provide useful information for both within-week and between-week changes in young soccer players.

records.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Wei, X, Zhu, H, Zheng, X, Gao, Y, Huang, J, Chen, X, Vigh-Larsen, JF, Mohr, M, and Krustrup, P. Greater reductions in deceleration compared with sprint ability following repeated high-intensity exercise in male and female soccer players, but no effect on countermovement jump (CMJ) or ball-kicking performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the acute effect of repeated sprint and deceleration on the fatigue of each component (sprint vs. deceleration) and on CMJ and soccer kicking performance, and to investigate the association between deceleration ability and fatigue. Thirty-three high-level male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) college soccer players completed 10 × 15-m sprints with subsequent 5-m enforced deceleration, interspersed with 20-s recovery intervals. Sprint and deceleration performance were measured continuously during the protocol, while CMJ and kicking performance were assessed before and immediately after. Furthermore, the players' deceleration ability was measured using deceleration deficit and deceleration index. Peak deceleration had significantly higher fatigue index (FI) and decrement score (Sdec) compared with speed (p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 3.18-3.32), while no significant decline was found in CMJ or kicking performance after the repeated sprint and deceleration protocol (p > 0.05, Cohen's d = -0.06∼0.23). A significant repeated sprint and deceleration × sex interaction effect was observed in peak ball speed (p < 0.05, ηp2 = 0.149), with women showing a decrease in peak ball speed compared with their male counterparts. The deceleration index correlated with FI and Sdec of speed (r = -0.444∼-0.516, p < 0.05), and the rate of CMJ decline correlated with FI and Sdec deceleration (r = 0.530-0.549, p < 0.05). Finally, the rate of decline in kicking speed was positively correlated with the Sdec deceleration rate (r = 0.423, p < 0.05). Deceleration capacity is more prone to acute fatigue than sprint ability. In addition, repeated sprint and deceleration had a limited effect on athletic performance, but men and women showed different adjusted trends in kicking speed. Finally, players having better deceleration capacity show a smaller performance drop.

records.title: Impact of Weekly Workload Distribution on Performance in Male Soccer Players Across Competitive Levels-Scientific Hypothesis or Empirical Evidence: A Systematic Review.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Impact of Weekly Workload Distribution on Performance in Male Soccer Players Across Competitive Levels-Scientific Hypothesis or Empirical Evidence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lafrance, G, Dupont, G, Ahmaidi, S, and Abaïdia, A. Impact of weekly workload distribution on performance in male soccer players across competitive levels-Scientific hypothesis or empirical evidence: A systematic review. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This systematic review aimed to analyze weekly workload distribution patterns in male soccer and examine their potential effects on performance outcomes. A systematic search was conducted using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science databases until December 2025. The analysis followed a 2-step approach: first, characterizing weekly workload distribution patterns within the microcycle, and second, examining available evidence on the potential effects of these distribution patterns on physical performance outcomes. Methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Forty-three studies met the inclusion criteria, with a moderate methodological quality score (5.09 ± 0.84/9). The synthesis identified a consistent weekly periodization model characterized by 3 phases: postmatch recovery (MD+1/MD+2), peak load distribution (MD-4/MD-3), and prematch tapering (MD-2/MD-1). Although this framework was common across teams, substantial observational differences in its practical implementation were reported. Regarding performance outcomes, only 2 studies (4.6%) examined the direct impact of load distribution through specific performance tests, providing limited evidence to establish clear relationships between training load patterns and physical performance. In conclusion, despite a common weekly framework, substantial differences in practical implementation across studies exist, and there is a critical lack of evidence regarding the impact of different load distribution strategies on performance outcomes. Future research should prioritize examining the relationship between weekly load distribution and performance to establish evidence-based recommendations for practitioners.

records.title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Relationships Between Isometric Belt Squat Force and Vertical Jump Performance Across Knee Joint Angles.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Rebelo, A, Ripley, N, Weakley, J, and Comfort, P. Relationships between isometric belt squat force and vertical jump performance across knee joint angles. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the relationships between vertical jump performance and isometric belt squat force assessed at 2 knee joint angles (120° and 90°) and to compare outcomes across age groups in male and female athletes. One hundred and twenty subjects (20.3 ± 6.5 years, 1.77 ± 0.12 m, 71.0 ± 13.3 kg) performed countermovement jumps, squat jumps, and isometric belt squat tests at 120° and 90° on dual force platforms. Between-group differences were analyzed using 1-way or Welch's analysis of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc analyses. Associations were examined using Pearson's correlations with Bonferroni-adjusted significance thresholds (p < 0.002), while omnibus tests used corrected alpha levels where applicable. Isometric belt squat net peak force demonstrated weak-to-moderate associations with jump height across tasks (r = 0.36-0.55). Associations between net force at 200 milliseconds and jump height were moderate at 90° (r = 0.45-0.52), whereas net force at 100 milliseconds showed negligible associations to jump height. Older athletes produced significantly higher absolute isometric net peak force than younger groups only at 90° knee flexion (up to ∼860 N difference), with moderate-to-large effects (g = 0.67-0.80), whereas relative net peak force did not differ between age categories. These findings indicate that the isometric belt squat can be confidently used to monitor maximal lower-limb force capacity across knee angles, with the 90° position offering greater sensitivity for distinguishing strength levels between age groups.

records.title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Relationship Between Objective Measures of Sleep and Nocturnal Cardiovascular Physiology and Swimming Performance in Collegiate Female Athletes: A Bayesian Analysis.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

records.title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Efficacy of a Meta-Analysis-Recommended Immersion Protocol vs. Field-Practical Cold-Water Immersion Protocol for Performance Recovery: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Kaji, R, Takeuchi, K, Okubo, S, and Yoshida, N. Efficacy of a meta-analysis-recommended immersion protocol vs. field-practical cold-water immersion protocol for performance recovery: A randomized crossover trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-We examined the effects of 2 cold-water immersion (CWI) protocols-15° C for 11 minutes and 10° C for 2.5 minutes-on performance recovery following exercise-induced fatigue. Fifteen male collegiate athletes completed 3 randomized crossover conditions with a 2-week washout: 15° C-11 minutes (evidence-based method), 10° C-2.5 minutes (field-practical method), and a seated-rest control. Outcomes included 20-m sprint time (T20), countermovement jump (CMJ), and Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 (YYIR2). The 20-m sprint time and CMJ were assessed before exercise (PreEx), immediately after exercise, immediately after the intervention, and at 1, 24, 48, and 72 hours postintervention, whereas YYIR2 was assessed at PreEx and at 72 hours postintervention. Physiological measures (tympanic temperature, skin temperatures, and heart rate) and perceptual measures (subjective fatigue and muscle soreness) were recorded. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol maintained T20 performance during the acute phase, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol facilitated later recovery. Countermovement jump performance transiently declined under both CWI conditions; however, a significant improvement at 72 hours occurred only with the 10° C-2.5-minute protocol. Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 performance did not differ between conditions. Thermal and cardiovascular responses varied by protocol and reflected recovery patterns. Subjective fatigue improved in both CWI conditions, whereas muscle soreness showed minimal differences. In conclusion, both evidence-based and field-practical CWI protocols enhanced recovery; however, they demonstrated distinct temporal profiles. The 10° C-2.5-minute protocol supported immediate restoration, whereas the 15° C-11-minute protocol promoted delayed recovery. For practical applications, protocol selection should align with sport-specific demands, recovery time, and performance objectives.

records.title: Effects of combined versus single supplementation of creatine and beta-alanine on aerobic and anerobic performance: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of combined versus single supplementation of creatine and beta-alanine on aerobic and anerobic performance: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Creatine (Cr) and β-alanine (BA) are among the most studied ergogenic supplements, acting on distinct physiological pathways-Cr facilitates phosphocreatine resynthesis and rapid ATP turnover, while BA elevates intramuscular carnosine to enhance acid-base buffering. Although both compounds improve high-intensity performance independently, the ergogenic potential of their combined use remains uncertain.

Objective

To systematically evaluate and compare the isolated and combined effects of Cr and BA supplementation on aerobic and anaerobic performance indices using a network meta-analytic approach.

Methods

Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (to August 2025) identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining Cr, BA, or Cr + BA supplementation (≥2 weeks) in healthy adult athletes. Fifty-two RCTs (PEDro ≥ 6) met the inclusion criteria. Standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were computed within random effects models. Performance outcomes included sprint, jump, agility, upper- and lower-body muscular endurance (UME, LME), and repeated-sprint ability (RSA).

Results

Cr supplementation significantly improved sprint performance (SMD = -0.64; p = 0.04), jump performance (SMD = 0.33; p = 0.002), RSA (SMD = -0.78; p = 0.01), and UME (SMD = 0.43; p = 0.01) versus placebo, with P scores ≥ 0.90 across these domains. In contrast, BA supplementation produced non-significant or context-specific effects, and combined Cr + BA showed no synergistic benefits. Agility and LME outcomes remained unaffected (p > 0.05). Heterogeneity ranged from low to moderate (I2 = 0-73%), with no global inconsistency or substantive publication bias.

Conclusion

Evidence indicates Cr supplementation alone yields the most consistent improvements in high-intensity and anaerobic performance by enhancing phosphocreatine recovery and neuromuscular output. BA's buffering advantage appears task-specific and insufficient to augment Cr's ergogenic efficacy. Co-supplementation of Cr and BA offers no additional advantage beyond Cr monotherapy. Standardized, long-term, multi-arm RCTs are warranted to further clarify potential interactive mechanisms and sex or sport-specific responses.

records.title: The effect of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep parameters in exercised population: a systematic review and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of randomized controlled trials.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effect of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep parameters in exercised population: a systematic review and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Background

Sleep is crucial for recovery and optimal performance in athletes; however, poor sleep is common during periods of intensive training or competition. The microbiota-gut-brain axis suggests probiotics and synbiotics could modulate sleep, but evidence in exercised populations is limited.

Objective

To systematically review randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of probiotic and synbiotic supplementation on sleep in exercised populations, using a Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) approach.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest were searched up to September 2025. Eligible studies were RCTs including exercised individuals, testing probiotics or synbiotics, and reporting sleep outcomes. Data extraction, risk of bias assessment (RoB 2), and narrative synthesis followed SWiM guidelines.

Results

Six RCTs (n = 180) were included: four probiotic and two synbiotic interventions lasting 4-17 weeks. Populations included athletes from multiple sports across four continents. Nine of twelve primary sleep outcomes favored supplementation, with significant effects for probiotics (combined p < 0.01) and synbiotics (p < 0.001). Benefits were most consistent for subjective sleep quality and, in some cases, sleep latency. Secondary outcomes showed occasional reductions in stress, anxiety, and fatigue.

Conclusion
